title: What Credit Score Do You Need for an Investment Property Loan?
excerpt: Your credit score plays a major role in qualifying for an investment property loan and determining your interest rate. This guide breaks down the exact numbers lenders look for and how to get approved even with less-than-perfect credit.
author: AIWholesail Team
tags: what credit score do you need for investment property loan
metaDescription: What credit score do you need for an investment property loan? Learn the minimum scores by loan type, tips to qualify, and alternatives for investors.
metaKeywords: what credit score do you need for investment property loan, investment property loan credit score, credit score for rental property, investment property financing, DSCR loan credit score, hard money loan credit score

sections.content: If you've ever tried to get a loan for an investment property, you already know it's a different game than buying a primary home. Lenders see rental properties and fix-and-flips as higher risk, so they hold borrowers to a tougher standard. One of the biggest questions new investors ask is: what credit score do you need for an investment property loan? The short answer is 620 at a minimum for most conventional loans, but 700 or higher gives you the best rates and the most options. Before we dig into the details, if you're still building your overall financing strategy, check out our complete resource on [How to Finance Real Estate Investments](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-financing) for a broader look at your options.
Why Lenders Have Higher Credit Score Requirements for Investment Properties

When you buy a home to live in, you're highly motivated to make your mortgage payment every month. When times get tough, most people will sacrifice other expenses before losing their primary residence. Investment properties are a different story. If a rental sits vacant for three months or a flip project runs over budget, some investors stop paying the loan. Lenders know this, which is why they charge higher interest rates and require stronger credit for investment properties compared to owner-occupied homes. They want to see that you have a strong history of managing debt responsibly before they hand over six figures on a property you won't even live in.
Credit Score Requirements by Loan Type
Conventional Loans (Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac)

Conventional loans are the most common option for investment properties with 1 to 4 units. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac set the guidelines that most banks and mortgage companies follow. For investment properties, they require a minimum credit score of 620. However, borrowers with scores between 620 and 679 will face significantly higher rates and may need to put 25% or more down. Borrowers with scores of 720 or above typically get the best pricing. It's also worth knowing that conventional lenders usually cap investors at 10 financed properties, so if you're scaling a portfolio, you'll eventually need to look at other loan types.
DSCR Loans (Debt Service Coverage Ratio)

DSCR loans have become extremely popular with real estate investors because they qualify you based on the rental income the property generates rather than your personal income. This makes them ideal for self-employed investors or anyone with a complex tax return. Most DSCR lenders require a credit score of at least 640 to 660, though some specialty lenders go as low as 620. Scores of 700 and above unlock better rates and lower reserve requirements. If this type of loan sounds like a fit for your strategy, read our full breakdown in [DSCR Loans Explained: Qualify Based on Rental Income](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/dscr-loans-explained).
Hard Money Loans

Hard money lenders are asset-based, meaning they care more about the value of the property than your personal credit. Many hard money lenders will work with borrowers who have scores as low as 550 to 580. Some don't check credit at all. The tradeoff is cost: interest rates typically run 10% to 15%, and loan terms are short, usually 6 to 24 months. These are best suited for fix-and-flip projects where you plan to sell or refinance quickly. If your credit is damaged and you need to get started now, hard money can be a real pathway into deals while you rebuild your score.
Portfolio Loans and Private Lenders

Portfolio lenders are banks or credit unions that keep loans on their own books instead of selling them to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. Because they set their own rules, requirements vary widely. Many are willing to work with borrowers with scores in the 620 to 660 range, especially if you have strong cash reserves, a low debt-to-income ratio, or an established relationship with the bank. Private lenders — individuals who lend their own money — often have the most flexibility of all, sometimes overlooking credit entirely in favor of a solid deal and a solid borrower relationship.

Before applying for any investment property loan, pull your credit report at AnnualCreditReport.com and dispute any errors. A single incorrect late payment or collection account could be dragging your score down 30 to 50 points — points that could cost you thousands in interest over the life of a loan.
How Your Credit Score Affects Your Interest Rate

The difference between a 640 credit score and a 740 credit score can mean a lot more than just getting approved. On a $250,000 investment property loan, a 1.5% difference in interest rate translates to roughly $230 more per month in mortgage payments. Over 30 years, that's over $82,000 in extra interest. Use the free [Mortgage Calculator at aiwholesail.com](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/mortgage-calculator) to run different rate scenarios based on your credit score range before you apply, so you know exactly what your cash flow will look like.
Minimum Credit Score Benchmarks at a Glance

items: Conventional loan (Fannie/Freddie): Minimum 620, best rates at 720+
DSCR loan: Minimum 620 to 660 depending on lender, best terms at 700+
FHA loan: 580 minimum, but only available for owner-occupied properties (not pure investment)
Hard money loan: 550 to 580 minimum, some lenders have no minimum
Portfolio loan: Varies by lender, typically 620 to 660
Private money: Often no hard minimum, relationship and deal quality matter most

sections.content: What to Do If Your Credit Score Isn't There Yet

A lower credit score doesn't have to mean sitting on the sidelines. Here are four practical steps to either improve your score or find a path forward right now. First, pay down revolving credit card balances below 30% of your credit limit. This alone can boost your score 20 to 50 points within 60 days. Second, avoid applying for new credit cards or loans in the six months before applying for a mortgage, since hard inquiries temporarily lower your score. Third, consider bringing in a co-borrower with strong credit who can help you qualify while you rebuild. Fourth, explore creative financing strategies like seller financing, subject-to deals, or joint ventures that don't require traditional credit approval. Our guide on [How to Invest in Real Estate With No Money Down](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/investing-no-money-down) covers many of these approaches in detail.

Another option investors often overlook is gap funding. If your credit is strong enough to secure primary financing but you're short on down payment funds, a gap funder can bridge that shortfall. Learn how it works in our article on [Gap Funding in Real Estate: What It Is and How to Get It](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/gap-funding-real-estate).

Credit is a tool, not a barrier. The investors who build strong portfolios aren't necessarily the ones who started with perfect scores — they're the ones who understood the rules of the game and played strategically.
Hot Markets Where Investors Are Closing Deals Right Now

Once your credit is in order and your financing strategy is set, the next step is finding the right market. Strong rental demand markets make it easier to hit the DSCR ratios lenders want to see, which can make the loan approval process smoother. Investors are currently seeing strong activity in markets like [Dallas, TX](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), [Atlanta, GA](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), and [Charlotte, NC](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/charlotte-nc), where rent growth supports solid debt coverage ratios.
